what_its_for: Methazolamide is used to lower the pressure inside your eyes. It is used to treat a type of glaucoma called open-angle glaucoma or before eye surgery. High pressure in the eye can damage your vision over time, and this medicine helps protect your eyesight.
how_to_take: Take methazolamide by mouth with a full glass of water. You can take it with food or milk if it upsets your stomach. Take it exactly as your doctor prescribed and try to take it at the same times each day. Do not crush or chew the tablets unless your doctor says it is okay.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 50 mg to 100 mg taken 2 to 3 times per day, depending on what your doctor decides is best for you. Your doctor may start you on a lower dose and adjust it over time. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions and never change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store methazolamide at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use this medicine after the expiration date printed on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking methazolamide because it can increase dizziness and other side effects. Be careful when driving or using machines, as this medicine may make you feel dizzy or drowsy. Avoid getting dehydrated — drink plenty of fluids unless your doctor tells you to limit fluids. Let your doctor know before taking any other medicines, vitamins, or supplements, as some can interact with methazolamide.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: severe skin rash, blistering, or peeling skin; difficulty breathing or swallowing; severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea; unusual bruising or bleeding; dark urine or yellowing of the skin or eyes (signs of liver problems); tingling or numbness in your hands or feet that is severe; signs of low potassium such as muscle cramps or weakness; kidney pain or blood in your urine; fever, chills, or sore throat that does not go away; or if your eye symptoms get worse instead of better.
when_it_works: Methazolamide usually begins to lower eye pressure within 2 to 4 hours after you take a dose. The full benefit may take a few days to a few weeks of regular use. Keep taking it even if you feel fine, because glaucoma often has no symptoms and the medicine works quietly in the background to protect your vision.
special_populations: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects like dizziness and should be careful to avoid falls. This medicine is generally not recommended during pregnancy unless clearly needed, so talk to your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. It may pass into breast milk, so discuss breastfeeding with your doctor before taking this medication. People with kidney disease, liver disease, or low sodium or potassium levels in their blood should use this medicine with caution and under close medical supervision. If you are allergic to sulfa drugs, tell your doctor before taking methazolamide, as there may be a risk of a similar reaction.
